Listen to this article Share African telecommunications operators seeking to expand Artificial Intelligence (AI) services could gain access to a new source of computing power as Cassava Technologies partners with Mauritius Telecom to extend the use of its NVIDIA-powered supercomputer and AI platforms across the continent. Advertisement Advertisement The partnership, formalised through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) at Africa Tech Festival in Cape Town, South Africa, on November 18, will explore access to Cassava’s AI Factory in Cape Town as an additional source of on-demand computing capacity for Mauritius Telecom’s artificial intelligence offerings. The development offers a potential route for telecom operators to scale AI services without relying exclusively on computing infrastructure within their home markets, as the cost and availability of advanced computing resources become increasingly important to the development and deployment of AI applications. Read also: Cassava Technologies expands AI infrastructure across Africa with NVIDIA-powered AI factories Under the agreement, Mauritius Telecom will also explore access to AI models through CAIMEx, Cassava’s AI platform. The additional computing and model access would complement MT’s existing myt AI Cloud platform and infrastructure in Mauritius, with the possibility of supporting its expansion into other African markets. Cassava describes its Cape Town AI Factory as Africa’s most powerful supercomputer, powered by NVIDIA technology. By combining this infrastructure with Mauritius Telecom’s AI products, local language capabilities and telecommunications experience, the companies are seeking to expand the availability of locally relevant AI services across African markets. Advertisement “Realising AI’s promise in Africa requires more than potential; it takes infrastructure, technology, and proven expertise. By pairing Mauritius Telecom’s AI products and operating experience with Cassava’s AI infrastructure and reach, we aim to bring locally relevant AI services and education solutions to more African markets,” said Ziaad Suleman, senior vice-president of Cassava Technologies for South Africa and Botswana. For Mauritius Telecom, the arrangement provides an opportunity to extend AI products developed in Mauritius beyond its domestic market by leveraging Cassava’s computing infrastructure and regional presence. Advertisement The company’s chief executive officer, Veemal Gungadin, said it was building AI capabilities in Mauritius that could also serve other African markets, pointing to its myt Learn platform as an example of how those capabilities were already being deployed in schools. The education platform, developed by Mauritius Telecom and currently rolling out in Mauritian schools for selected grades, provides curriculum-aligned lessons, a multilingual AI tutor and personalised revision. It also gives teachers access to student performance insights and AI tools for marking, test creation and lesson preparation. Advertisement Advertisement The companies will jointly assess opportunities to introduce myt Learn into South Africa’s public and private education sectors before considering expansion into other markets where Cassava operates. However, access to Cassava’s computing capacity and AI models will depend on customer permission for the relevant workloads, according to the companies. This means the proposed arrangement is not an automatic transfer of customer data or workloads to Cassava’s infrastructure. The partnership comes as African technology companies and telecom operators explore ways to overcome infrastructure constraints that could limit the development of locally built AI products. Access to high-performance computing, AI models and cloud infrastructure remains an important requirement for organisations seeking to deploy AI applications at scale. Read also: Cassava Technologies becomes authorised reseller of Anthropic’s Claude AI in Africa For telecom operators, the opportunity extends beyond providing connectivity to building and distributing AI-powered services for consumers, businesses and public institutions. Partnerships that combine computing infrastructure with locally developed applications could help reduce some of the barriers to entering the market. Cassava and Mauritius Telecom said their collaboration would demonstrate how telecommunications operators could bring locally relevant AI services to customers while taking African-developed products into new markets. The proposed expansion will depend on the outcome of the companies’ assessments, including the suitability of their platforms for different markets, local education requirements and the computing needs of future AI services.
